paragraphs: Researchers can now stimulate selected groups of individual neurons with light while measuring activity across a neural population. This creates an experimental design problem: there are many possible groups to stimulate, and collecting responses takes time. The paper asks how to choose stimulation patterns that provide the most useful information for learning how population activity evolves.

The authors first demonstrate the effectiveness of a low-rank linear dynamical model using responses to photostimulation in mouse motor cortex. They then develop an active learning procedure that uses the model’s low-rank structure to select informative groups of neurons. The selection strategy is built on a new method for active learning in low-rank regression.

Evaluations on real and synthetic data show that this targeted selection can reduce the measurements needed for a given level of predictive performance. In some cases, the required data falls by as much as half. The contribution connects experimental control with model learning, making the choice of which neurons to stimulate part of the effort to understand their collective dynamics.
neurips-2024-active-learning-of-neural-p.tldr: An active learning method selects informative neuron stimulation patterns, sometimes halving the data needed to predict neural population activity.

paragraphs: A multiplex graph represents several kinds of relationships among nodes. Learning from these graphs without labels requires deciding which connections and information to preserve. The paper identifies two problems with existing approaches: unreliable connections introduce irrelevant noise, and emphasizing agreement between graphs can overlook useful information that appears in only one relationship type.

InfoMGF learns a fused graph while refining the structures of its component graphs. Its objective preserves both information shared across views and information unique to individual views, while removing task-irrelevant noise. This matters when the different relationship types contribute complementary evidence, rather than largely repeating the same information.

The authors provide theoretical analyses supporting the framework and evaluate it across multiple downstream tasks. They report stronger performance and robustness than the compared baselines, including better results than sophisticated supervised approaches in their evaluation. These findings support treating graph quality and view-specific information as central parts of unsupervised fusion, rather than assuming that the original connections are reliable or that agreement captures everything useful.
neurips-2024-beyond-redundancy-informati.tldr: InfoMGF improves unsupervised graph fusion by removing irrelevant connections while preserving both shared and view-specific useful information.

paragraphs: Gaussian processes offer predictions with uncertainty estimates, but choosing their model settings becomes expensive as datasets grow. Approximate computations reduce the workload while introducing error. Earlier computation-aware methods explicitly represented that error as computational uncertainty, allowing a tradeoff between precision and effort, but still required quadratic computational complexity.

This paper extends computation-aware Gaussian processes to model selection and develops an approach with linear scaling in dataset size. A new training loss supports hyperparameter optimization within this framework. The aim is to make model fitting practical on large datasets while retaining uncertainty information that could otherwise be weakened by approximation.

Experiments show that the method can outperform SGPR, CGGP, and SVGP on medium to large datasets. The authors also demonstrate model selection on 1.8 million observations within a few hours using one GPU. These results indicate that explicitly accounting for computational approximation can be compatible with large-scale training, without significantly compromising the uncertainty quantification that makes Gaussian processes useful for decision-making.
neurips-2024-computation-aware-gaussian-.tldr: A computation-aware Gaussian process method enables linear-time scaling for model selection while preserving useful uncertainty estimates.

paragraphs: Auditory attention detection uses brain signals to identify which speaker a person is attending to. The paper argues that existing methods underuse the spatial arrangement of EEG activity and struggle to capture dependencies spanning longer periods. Both shortcomings restrict how effectively a model can interpret the recorded brain activity.

DARNet addresses these issues through three connected modules. First, a spatiotemporal construction module builds representations that include the spatial distribution of EEG signals. A dual attention refinement module then extracts temporal patterns at different levels and captures longer-range dependencies. Finally, a fusion and classification module combines this information to identify the attended speaker.

Experiments report strong classification performance, particularly when decisions use short windows of EEG data. The network also uses 91% fewer parameters than the state-of-the-art models used for comparison while maintaining excellent classification performance. The findings suggest that explicitly organizing spatial and temporal information can support effective attention detection with a substantially smaller model, including when little time is available for each decision.
neurips-2024-darnet-dual-attention-refin.tldr: DARNet combines spatial EEG structure with temporal attention to detect attended speakers using substantially fewer model parameters.

paragraphs: Serving several fine-tuned language models can require storing many versions of a shared base model. One strategy stores the base once and compresses each model’s delta weights, which describe its changes from that base. The authors observe that existing low-rank and low-bit compression methods can substantially damage the performance of specialized models, including models tuned for mathematics.

Delta-CoMe uses mixed precision to compress these differences without additional training. Its design follows the observed long-tailed distribution of singular values in delta weights. Singular vectors associated with larger singular values receive higher-bit representations, allocating precision unevenly according to this structure rather than treating all components alike.

Evaluations cover mathematics, coding, chat, and vision-language models. The authors report performance comparable to the full fine-tuned models and considerably better than the tested low-rank and low-bit alternatives. Compatibility with Llama-2, Llama-3, and Mistral further supports the approach’s applicability across backbones. The findings show that how precision is distributed within a delta can matter greatly for preserving specialized capabilities.
neurips-2024-delta-come-training-free-de.tldr: Delta-CoMe compresses fine-tuning changes with mixed precision, preserving specialized model performance better than tested low-rank and low-bit alternatives.

paragraphs: The paper tests whether restricting a predictor to features that causally influence its target improves performance in new domains. It examines 16 tabular prediction tasks spanning health, employment, education, social benefits, and politics. Each dataset contains multiple domains, making it possible to compare performance within the training domain and after transfer elsewhere.

For every task, the researchers select causal features and compare models using those features with models using all available features. Across all tasks evaluated, the all-feature predictors achieve higher accuracy both within and outside the training domain. Causal predictors also show no advantage in the absolute accuracy loss associated with moving between domains.

Additional comparisons find that recent causal domain-generalization methods do not outperform standard predictors trained on the selected causal features. Causal discovery algorithms either fail to run or identify variables that perform no better than the authors’ selection. Robustness checks show stability under variable misclassification. Together, these empirical findings challenge the proposed advantage of causal feature restriction in the settings studied, without establishing a universal conclusion about every domain shift.
neurips-2024-do-causal-predictors-genera.tldr: Across 16 evaluated tasks, predictors using all available features outperform causal-feature predictors both within and across domains.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks used for social media tasks can be attacked by changing graph connections. Platforms may already possess examples of such attack sequences from automated and manual screening. This paper studies how to turn a limited collection of observed attacks into a learned attack policy that supplies additional examples for strengthening detection models.

The method combines maximum entropy inverse reinforcement learning with a mixture of experts to accommodate attacks from multiple sources. It reconstructs attack behavior and provides explanations at the feature level. Precise sample guidance and a bidirectional update mechanism address deviations caused by imperfect feature representations and negative sampling in the large space of possible graph actions, while speeding policy learning.

Experiments target rumor-detection GNNs on real-world datasets. Using a small subset of examples from several attack methods, the learned policy closely approximates the original attacks’ performance. Samples generated from that policy then improve detector robustness through adversarial training and data augmentation. The contribution is a way to reuse observed attack behavior as a source of further defensive training data.
neurips-2024-enhancing-robustness-of-gra.tldr: A mixture-of-experts inverse reinforcement learning method reconstructs graph attacks and generates training examples that improve rumor-detector robustness.

paragraphs: Generating useful synthetic tables requires producing examples that represent every class, including classes with few observations in the original data. This paper examines how the examples and formatting inside a language model’s prompt affect that task. Its focus is on using in-context learning to guide generation of realistic tabular records.

The proposed approach, EPIC, brings together balanced examples, grouped samples, consistent formatting, and a unique mapping for variables. These prompt design choices guide the model toward accurate synthetic data across classes, even when the underlying dataset is imbalanced. The method therefore treats the organization of the prompt as a central part of the data-generation process.

Evaluations on real-world datasets report state-of-the-art downstream classification performance alongside significantly improved generation efficiency. The classification results matter because they connect the generated tables to their usefulness for machine learning, beyond simply describing the output as realistic. The findings support carefully structured prompting as an effective approach to synthetic tabular data generation, particularly when uneven class representation is a concern.
neurips-2024-epic-effective-prompting-fo.tldr: EPIC uses balanced examples and consistent prompt structure to generate synthetic tabular data that improves classification on imbalanced datasets.

paragraphs: This paper studies hallucination in in-context learning, where a generative model receives a dataset and a prediction question. Its starting point is a Bayesian interpretation: the model behaves as though it predicts using an unknown probabilistic model connecting observed datasets with hidden mechanisms. That interpretation supplies a specific meaning for hallucination.

Under this perspective, a hallucination is a generated answer with low likelihood given the underlying mechanism. The authors develop a method for estimating the probability of such an answer for a particular in-context learning problem. The method requires generating prediction questions and responses from the model and evaluating the log probabilities of its responses.

The authors empirically evaluate the estimator using language models on synthetic regression and natural-language in-context learning tasks. The contribution is a way to estimate a hallucination rate through model generation and probability evaluation within the stated probabilistic framework. Because the definition is tied to likelihood under a mechanism, its interpretation depends on that framework rather than automatically covering every everyday use of the word hallucination.
neurips-2024-estimating-the-hallucinatio.tldr: A Bayesian framework estimates in-context hallucination rates using generated questions, responses, and response log probabilities.

paragraphs: The paper investigates whether a trained neural network can learn internal look-ahead, rather than relying entirely on simple heuristics. Its subject is Leela Chess Zero’s policy and value network. Because the network processes chessboard squares as transformer tokens, the researchers can examine how information about particular squares contributes to decisions.

Three findings support learned look-ahead. Activations at some squares associated with future moves have unusually strong causal importance. Certain attention heads carry important information between squares involved in earlier and later moves. A simple probe also predicts the optimal move two turns ahead with 92% accuracy, specifically in positions where Leela identifies a single best continuation.

Together, these observations indicate that the network represents future optimal moves and that those representations are crucial to its output in certain board states. The causal evidence strengthens the interpretation beyond merely finding future-move information that a probe can read. The result provides evidence of learned look-ahead in this network, with the reported probe accuracy tied to the stated subset of positions.
neurips-2024-evidence-of-learned-look-ah.tldr: Analysis of Leela Chess Zero finds causally important future-move representations, providing evidence that its neural network has learned look-ahead.

paragraphs: The paper argues that widely used AI benchmarks often fail to serve the development of language tools for Indigenous communities. Their emphasis on general-purpose systems can overlook the needs of particular languages. The authors identify problems including grammatical and spelling errors, poor pronunciation, restricted vocabulary, and content that lacks relevance to the community’s culture.

They create a dataset for te reo Māori, the Indigenous language of Aotearoa/New Zealand, with the aim of evaluating tools against community purposes. The work presents tailored benchmark development as a way to connect data quality and evaluation choices with the language tools that a community actually wants to build.

The proposed approach considers the effects of colonisation, represents diversity among speakers, and supports community aspirations for tools and language revitalisation. Its contribution is a demonstration of how a low-resource Indigenous language can develop a high-quality benchmark around those priorities. Evaluation becomes a means of supporting a language community’s goals, with success defined in relation to those goals.
neurips-2024-fit-for-our-purpose-not-you.tldr: A te reo Māori dataset demonstrates benchmark design centered on Indigenous language communities, speaker diversity, and revitalisation goals.

paragraphs: Time series can change through both evolving trends and shifting seasonal patterns. Existing reversible instance normalization methods use statistics such as mean and variance to reduce the effects of changing trends. The paper argues that this captures only basic trend behavior and does not adequately handle seasonal structure.

Frequency adaptive normalization, or FAN, uses the Fourier transform to identify the predominant frequency components of each input instance. These components capture most of the non-stationary factors in the proposed approach. A simple multilayer perceptron explicitly predicts how those components differ between the observed input and the future output, extending normalization to changing trends and seasonal patterns.

FAN is designed to work with arbitrary forecasting backbones. The authors evaluate it with four forecasting models across eight benchmark datasets and report average mean squared error improvements ranging from 7.76% to 37.90%. These results support modeling the evolution of dominant frequencies as a useful addition to forecasting, while the backbone-independent design makes the approach applicable beyond a single forecasting architecture.
neurips-2024-frequency-adaptive-normaliz.tldr: FAN improves time-series forecasting by normalizing and predicting changes in dominant frequencies that capture trends and seasonal patterns.

paragraphs: Few-shot point-cloud segmentation assigns semantic classes to 3D points using only a few annotated examples. Prototype methods summarize each class from those examples and use the summaries to label a new cloud. Their effectiveness can suffer when the examples contain limited semantic information or represent classes differently from the query cloud.

GPCPR improves these summaries using two sources of additional information. One component incorporates varied class descriptions generated by a language model, enriching the prototypes’ semantic content. Another aggregates reliable class-specific context from pseudo predictions on the query, adapting prototypes to that particular cloud. A dual-distillation regularizer also transfers knowledge between earlier and deeper prototypes or pseudo predictions.

Experiments report gains over state-of-the-art methods of up to 12.10% mIoU on S3DIS and 13.75% on ScanNet. The results support combining descriptive class knowledge with evidence from the actual query. These sources address different weaknesses: generated descriptions broaden what a prototype expresses, while query context helps account for differences between the labeled examples and the cloud being segmented.
neurips-2024-generated-and-pseudo-conten.tldr: GPCPR improves few-shot 3D segmentation by refining class prototypes with language-model descriptions and reliable context from the query cloud.

paragraphs: Adversarial training seeks models that remain reliable when inputs are deliberately perturbed. This paper analyzes its statistical behavior in high-dimensional linear regression, focusing on perturbations bounded in the infinity norm. The analysis is non-asymptotic, providing prediction-error guarantees for finite samples rather than relying only on behavior as the sample size grows indefinitely.

For sparse regression parameters, the authors show that adversarial training can attain the minimax prediction-error rate up to a logarithmic factor. This result requires the restricted eigenvalue condition. The guarantee therefore links adversarial training to near-optimal statistical accuracy under a stated structural assumption, beyond its motivation as a way to resist perturbations.

The paper also analyzes a group version of adversarial training. Under certain group-sparsity patterns, this version has a better upper bound on prediction error than classical adversarial training. The qualification matters: the improvement is established for particular patterns of grouped sparsity. Together, the results characterize when adversarial training has strong prediction guarantees and when incorporating group structure sharpens those guarantees.
neurips-2024-high-dimensional-group-adve.tldr: Under stated structural conditions, adversarial training achieves near-minimax regression error, with sharper bounds for certain group-sparse settings.

paragraphs: Token-based image generators rely on a tokenizer to turn images into sequences of discrete representations. Such tokenizers are commonly trained to reconstruct pixels. This paper asks whether knowledge learned for image understanding can produce better tokens for generation, exploring a direction complementary to using generative models for understanding tasks.

The proposed approach trains tokenizers to reconstruct features by distilling knowledge from pretrained image-understanding encoders. Comparisons across metrics, datasets, tasks, and proposal networks find that tokenizers with stronger understanding capabilities produce better generation results. The authors also present a straightforward pipeline for converting image-understanding encoders directly into tokenizers.

One reported result is an FID of 4.10 on ImageNet-1k for VQ-KD CLIP. Visualizations suggest that rich semantic information in the VQ-KD codebook partly explains its advantage; this is a suggested explanation rather than a complete causal account. Overall, the findings support feature reconstruction as a useful tokenizer objective and show that representations developed for understanding images can also improve how images are generated.
neurips-2024-image-understanding-makes-f.tldr: Training image tokenizers to reconstruct features from understanding models improves image generation across the evaluated settings.

paragraphs: Kernel methods can represent learned functions linearly while retaining substantial expressive power. Requiring every output to be non-negative complicates that combination: existing approaches often retain linearity with limited flexibility or gain flexibility through nonlinear representations. This paper investigates whether linear representations and universal approximation can coexist with the non-negativity constraint.

The main result gives a sufficient condition on a positive definite kernel for constructing flexible linear approximators of non-negative functions. The authors call kernels with these properties inverse M-kernels. For one-dimensional inputs, they establish that universal exponential, or Abel, kernels satisfy the condition and yield linear universal approximators with non-negative outputs.

Experiments examine non-negativity-constrained regression, density estimation, and intensity estimation, supporting the usefulness of the theoretical results. The established universal construction is specifically for one-dimensional input spaces; the paper separately discusses issues and prospects for higher dimensions. The contribution is an existence result and a constructive route showing that non-negativity need not force the usual tradeoff between linear representation and approximation power in this setting.
neurips-2024-inverse-m-kernels-for-linea.tldr: Inverse M-kernels provide sufficient conditions for flexible linear non-negative approximators, including universal constructions for one-dimensional inputs.

paragraphs: Robot policy learning is constrained by the scarcity of videos paired with action labels. Human videos offer abundant examples of physical activity, but transferring their information is difficult because humans and robots differ and video dynamics are noisy and multimodal. This paper connects learning from actionless human videos with learning robot actions from limited demonstrations.

The framework first compresses human and robot videos into a shared form of video tokens. During pretraining, a discrete diffusion model uses a mask-and-replace strategy to predict future tokens in that latent representation. During fine-tuning, the resulting imagined future videos guide low-level action learning using a small collection of robot videos with action labels.

Experiments show high-fidelity future-video generation for planning and stronger fine-tuned policies than the compared state-of-the-art approaches. The key connection is that future prediction learned from human video becomes guidance for action learning. Robot demonstrations still supply action information, while the large actionless collection supports learning about how scenes and interactions can develop over time.
neurips-2024-learning-an-actionable-disc.tldr: A shared discrete diffusion framework transfers future-video prediction from actionless human videos into robot policies trained with limited labeled demonstrations.

paragraphs: This paper studies the statistical and computational behavior of latent diffusion transformers under the assumption that data occupy a low-dimensional linear latent space. It asks how well their score networks can approximate the required functions, how much data learning needs, and when inference and training can be computationally efficient.

Under additional mild data assumptions, the authors derive a score-network approximation bound that grows sublinearly with latent dimension, together with a sample-complexity bound. They also show that generation using the estimated score converges toward a region near the original data distribution. This is a qualified distribution-recovery result within the assumed setting.

For computation, the analysis uses the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis to characterize hardness and identify efficient inference criteria. The authors demonstrate almost-linear inference and develop almost-linear training through chained low-rank approximations to gradients with bounded error. Across these results, the subspace dimension dominates statistical rates and computational efficiency. The theory therefore suggests a route around high ambient dimensionality when the low-dimensional linear-space assumption applies.
neurips-2024-on-statistical-rates-and-pr.tldr: Under a low-dimensional linear latent-space assumption, the paper derives statistical guarantees and criteria for almost-linear latent diffusion transformer computation.

paragraphs: Vision-language models commonly learn image-text alignment by giving every text token equal treatment during autoregressive training. The paper argues that this can place too much emphasis on words that have little connection to the image, or even contradict it. Equal weighting can therefore weaken the connection between visual evidence and the language being learned.

Contrastive Alignment, or CAL, assigns different training weights according to each token’s visual correlation. To estimate that correlation, the method contrasts image inputs and examines how the prediction logits for each token change. Those differences provide a signal for identifying tokens whose predictions are more closely connected to the visual input.

Experiments show consistent improvements across different types of vision-language models, image resolutions, model sizes, and benchmark datasets. The authors also report minimal additional computational overhead, making the method efficient relative to alternative data-scaling strategies. The finding supports improving alignment through a more selective training signal: the method changes which tokens receive emphasis based on their relationship to the image.
neurips-2024-seeing-the-image-prioritizi.tldr: CAL improves vision-language alignment by weighting text tokens according to how strongly their predictions depend on the image.

paragraphs: The minimum-cost reach-avoid problem asks an agent to reach a goal, avoid unsafe states, and minimize accumulated cost subject to those requirements. The paper explains that the structure of this problem is incompatible with existing reinforcement-learning methods. A common workaround combines the different objectives into a weighted sum, but that surrogate can produce policies that do not directly minimize the intended cumulative cost.

The authors propose RC-PPO to address the original problem using connections to Hamilton-Jacobi reachability. This connection provides the basis for a reinforcement-learning method organized around reaching the goal safely while minimizing cost. The distinction matters because the original formulation treats reaching and avoiding as constraints on the cost-minimization problem.

On a suite of MuJoCo minimum-cost reach-avoid benchmarks, RC-PPO learns policies with goal-reaching rates comparable to existing methods while reducing cumulative costs by up to 57%. These empirical results show an advantage in the measured cost objective without a corresponding loss in reported goal-reaching performance. The stated reduction is the largest observed improvement, rather than a uniform gain across every benchmark.
neurips-2024-solving-minimum-cost-reach-.tldr: RC-PPO targets minimum-cost reach-avoid directly, achieving comparable goal-reaching rates with up to 57% lower costs in MuJoCo benchmarks.

paragraphs: Survival models need to distinguish patients with different outcomes while producing well-calibrated predictions. Previous deep-learning approaches often improve discrimination through ranking losses, but that improvement can come at the expense of calibration. This paper seeks a training approach that strengthens discrimination while preserving the quality of the predicted probabilities.

The proposed contrastive-learning method uses weighted sampling and assigns smaller penalties to samples with similar survival outcomes. Its design follows the assumption that patients with similar event times have similar clinical statuses. Combined with a standard negative log-likelihood loss, it improves discrimination without directly manipulating the model outputs, supporting better calibration.

Experiments on multiple real-world clinical datasets report better discrimination and calibration than the state-of-the-art deep survival models used for comparison. Quantitative and qualitative ablation studies further support the method’s effectiveness. The findings indicate that outcome-aware learning can improve both evaluation goals together in the tested settings, with the relationship between event-time similarity and clinical similarity providing the stated rationale for how samples are treated.
neurips-2024-toward-a-well-calibrated-di.tldr: Outcome-aware contrastive learning improves survival-model discrimination and calibration by treating patients with similar event times more similarly.

paragraphs: Domain generalization aims to learn from available domains and perform well on unseen ones. This paper focuses on frequency shortcuts: models may rely too heavily on particular spatial frequency components instead of semantic information. The authors argue that some augmentation methods can encourage additional shortcuts, creating apparent generalization improvements without resolving this underlying behavior.

Their theoretical account connects biased learning across frequencies to the frequency statistics of the dataset. From this perspective, changing the dataset’s structure in the Fourier domain can influence which components a model learns to depend on. Dominant and highly dependent frequency components are identified as places where shortcuts can reside.

The proposed method uses two cooperating data-augmentation modules to adaptively adjust those frequency characteristics. By dynamically perturbing components on which the model over-relies, the approach aims to discourage shortcut use during learning. Its contribution is a data-driven strategy for influencing frequency dependence, supported by the stated theoretical justification. The intended benefit is more transferable learning through changes to the statistics of the training data.
neurips-2024-towards-combating-frequency.tldr: Two adaptive augmentation modules alter dataset frequency statistics to discourage frequency shortcuts and support domain generalization.

paragraphs: Implicit neural representations encode a signal in a neural network, supporting applications such as compression and interpolation at new coordinates. Once trained, however, their internal organization can make ordinary editing operations difficult. This paper focuses on cropping: removing part of an encoded signal while also reducing the network that stores it.

Local-Global SIRENs combine local and global feature extraction in an architecture designed to support this operation. A selected portion of the signal can be removed by deleting its corresponding network weights, without retraining. The decrease in weights is proportional to the removed portion, connecting the extent of the crop to a reduction in representation size.

The authors also show how the architecture supports extending previously encoded signals. Beyond editing, they examine faster training, better encoding of different signals, improved downstream performance, and application of the local-global approach to INCODE. The central contribution is architectural: organizing the representation so that meaningful signal edits correspond to direct changes in the network’s stored weights.
neurips-2024-towards-croppable-implicit-.tldr: Local-Global SIRENs enable cropping encoded signals by deleting corresponding network weights, proportionally shrinking the representation without retraining.

paragraphs: Prediction-set decision support gives a human expert several candidate labels and asks them to choose among those options. This paper studies how to construct sets that maximize the expert’s average accuracy. It first shows that sets produced by conformal prediction are generally suboptimal for this particular human-performance objective.

Finding the optimal sets is computationally difficult: the problem is NP-hard, and unless P equals NP, approximating it within any factor smaller than the number of labels is also hard. The authors nevertheless introduce an efficient greedy method. For a broad class of expert models and non-conformity scores, it guarantees performance at least as good as that obtained with conformal prediction sets.

Simulations using both synthetic and real expert predictions show that the greedy algorithm finds near-optimal sets and improves performance over conformal prediction in practice. The contribution connects the design of candidate sets to the behavior of the person selecting the final label. Its theoretical guarantee applies to the specified class of models and scores, while near-optimality is reported empirically.
neurips-2024-towards-human-ai-complement.tldr: An efficient greedy algorithm constructs prediction sets that improve human classification accuracy, with conditional guarantees over conformal prediction.

paragraphs: Online convex optimization algorithms must make repeated decisions while the type of loss function may be uncertain. Universal algorithms adapt across several convex function classes, but leading methods typically require a logarithmic number of projections onto the feasible domain each round. When that domain is complicated, these repeated projections can be expensive.

The paper develops algorithms requiring only one such projection per round. They use a surrogate loss over simpler domains, maintain experts for different function types, and combine the experts through a meta-algorithm. A specially designed loss for strongly convex functions follows from separating regret into the contributions of the meta-algorithm and individual experts.

The analysis controls the difference between regret for the original and surrogate losses, yielding optimal regret bounds simultaneously for general convex, exponentially concave, and strongly convex functions. A further modification uses smoothness to obtain small-loss regret for multiple convex and smooth function classes. The result reduces the costly projection requirement while retaining the stated theoretical guarantees across several types of online problems.
neurips-2024-universal-online-convex-opt.tldr: Universal online optimization algorithms achieve optimal regret across several convex function classes using only one domain projection per round.
